e.etymology: An English surname from Old French burel, a coarse brown woolen cloth, given to someone who made or wore it.
A spelling of Arlene, a name of unclear origin whose early form Arline was the heroine of the 1843 opera The Bohemian Girl.
A pet form of names ending in -zetta or -etta, such as Rosetta and Izetta.
In 19th-century America a first name of unclear origin, found mostly in West Virginia. Okey is also an Igbo short form of Okechukwu, God's portion.
e.note: Sounds like okay, and like Okie, a sometimes derogatory word for an Oklahoman.

e.etymology: A spelling of Gary, from an English surname that goes back to a Norman name built on Germanic ger, spear. The actor Gary Cooper made Gary a first name in the 1920s and 1930s.
A short form of Cordelia, the name of King Lear's loyal daughter. It is often linked with Latin cor, heart.
From a misreading of Nerthus, the earth goddess of Germanic tribes described by the Roman historian Tacitus. The name was popular in Germany in the 19th century.
An English surname brought by the Normans, either from the Germanic name Gifard, gift and brave, or from an Old French nickname for a chubby-cheeked man.
The short form of Deborah, Hebrew for bee, the name of a prophetess and judge of Israel in the Old Testament.
A form of Italian Antonietta, a diminutive of Antonia, the feminine of the Roman family name Antonius, whose meaning is unknown.
A misspelling of Deborah, Hebrew for bee, the name of a prophetess and judge of Israel in the Old Testament.
A spelling of Darryl, from the English surname Darrell, brought by Normans who came from Airelle in Calvados, France.
From the Germanic words ragin, counsel, and wald, rule. Reynold, Reginald and Ronald come from the same roots.
From the Scottish surname Chalmers, the Scots form of chamber, given to an officer who ran a noble household's private rooms.
A misspelling of Clarence, from the English royal title Duke of Clarence, created in 1362 and named for the town of Clare in Suffolk.
The older spelling of Wilfred, from Old English wil, will or desire, and frith, peace. Saint Wilfrid was a 7th-century bishop of York.
A phonetic spelling of Sade, the stage name of the singer Helen Folasade Adu, whose mid-1980s hits started the name in America. Sade is short for Yoruba Folasade, honor earns a crown.
From the Germanic words adal, noble, and wolf. It was a common German and Scandinavian name until the Second World War.

assoc.t: Adolf Hitler, Nazi dictator of Germany

e.note: Inseparable from Adolf Hitler; the name has been all but abandoned since World War II.

e.etymology: A run-together form of the double name Betty Lou, joining the pet forms of Elizabeth and Louise. Double names of this kind were at their height in the 1920s and 1930s.
A spelling of Mona, the English form of Irish Muadhnait, from muadh, noble. Monna is also an old Italian title for a lady, as in Monna Lisa, the Italian name of the Mona Lisa.
A spelling of Roseanne, a compound of Rose and Anne. Rose is the flower name; Anne comes from Hebrew Hannah, grace.
A spelling of Marilyn, a 20th-century blend of Mary and the -lyn ending.
A spelling of Wendy, the name J. M. Barrie made famous in Peter Pan (1904), taken from a child's nickname for him, fwendy.
A Scandinavian short form of Ingegerd or Ingrid, Old Norse names built on the god-name Ing. The Swedish-born actress Inger Stevens made it known in America in the 1960s.
A form of Rollo, the Latinized name of the Viking Hrolf who founded Normandy, from Norse words for fame and wolf. It also served as a pet form of Roland.
A spelling of Lorene, an elaboration of Lora or Laura, from Latin laurus, the laurel tree.
